title: The Sanctuary and the Most Holy Place
summary: The guide brings Ezekiel into the temple building itself. He measures the outer sanctuary, then goes alone into the inner room and names it the Most Holy Place. The chapter describes the thick walls and three stories of side rooms around the temple, a large building to the west, the wood paneling, the carvings of cherubim and palm trees, a wooden altar called the table before the LORD, and the double doors of the sanctuary.
story: Chapter 40 brought the prophet through the gates and courts to the porch of the temple. Now he reaches the heart of the complex, the rooms where God's presence was believed to dwell. The last time Ezekiel saw the inside of a temple in vision, its walls were carved with creeping things and detestable beasts and its rooms were full of idolatry (8:10). Here the walls carry only cherubim and palm trees, the imagery of Eden and of the tabernacle. The sanctuary is ready, but it is still empty; the glory of the LORD will not enter until chapter 43.
historical:
The proportions follow Solomon's temple, which Ezekiel, a priest born in Jerusalem, likely knew before his exile in 597 BC. Solomon's main hall was forty cubits long and twenty wide, and the inner sanctuary a cube of twenty cubits (1 Kings 6:2, 17, 20), matching Ezekiel's measurements. Solomon's temple also had three stories of side rooms around it, supported on ledges so that beams would not be inserted into the temple walls (1 Kings 6:5-6), exactly the arrangement described in verse 6. The carved cherubim and palm trees also appear in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:29).

This three-room plan (porch, main hall, inner room) was not unique to Israel. Excavated temples in Syria from the early first millennium BC, such as the one at Ain Dara, share the same basic layout. What made Israel's temple different was not its architecture but its worship: no image of God stood in its inner room.
cultural:
Temples in the ancient world were understood as the dwelling of a deity, and holiness intensified toward the innermost room. In Israel only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Ezekiel honors that boundary: in verse 3 the guide goes in alone, and the prophet, though a priest, stays outside and hears it named. In Solomon's temple that room had held the ark of the covenant beneath two great cherubim. Ezekiel's vision mentions no ark, no lampstand, and no incense altar; only the wooden table "before the LORD" (verse 22), probably the table for the bread of the Presence (Exodus 25:23-30).

Cherubim were winged guardian figures, common in ancient Near Eastern art at thresholds and thrones. In the Bible they guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24) and flank God's throne. Palm trees suggested fruitfulness and life. Together they made the temple a picture of Eden, the garden where God once walked with humanity. The two-faced cherubim here (verses 18 to 19) differ from the four-faced living creatures of chapters 1 and 10, perhaps because a flat carving could show only two faces.
literary: The chapter continues the guided tour but changes its pace. The first four verses move quickly inward, and the dimensions shrink as holiness increases: an entrance of ten cubits, then six; a room of forty by twenty, then twenty by twenty. The guide speaks only twice, to name the Most Holy Place (verse 4) and the table before the LORD (verse 22). The rest of the chapter circles outward again to describe the side rooms, the western building, and the decoration. Some details of the Hebrew in verses 7 to 11 and 15 to 17 are obscure, and translations differ in how they reconstruct the structures, which is one reason drawings of Ezekiel's temple vary.

outline.t: The inner sanctuary: the Most Holy Place
The temple walls and the three stories of side rooms
The western building and the overall measurements
Galleries, paneling, and carved cherubim and palm trees
The wooden altar: the table before the LORD

doctrines.note: The guide enters the Most Holy Place alone and the prophet remains outside (verses 3 to 4). The chapter preserves the distance between God's holiness and human access, even in a vision of restoration.

The cherubim and palm trees that cover the walls recall the garden of Eden. The temple is a small world where God's presence dwells, a sign of his intention to dwell with humanity in a restored creation.
The carvings here replace the idolatrous images Ezekiel saw on the temple walls in 8:10. The restored sanctuary has no image of God and no rival to him.

words.note: Qodesh, holiness; in the phrase "Most Holy Place" (literally holy of holies), it names the innermost room, the place of God's special presence. The Hebrew doubles the word to express the highest degree.
Hekhal, the temple's main hall or nave, here translated outer sanctuary. The word can also mean palace, and it was used for the dwelling of a king. God's house is a royal palace.
Kerub, cherub. Winged guardian beings associated with God's throne and with the boundary of Eden. Their carved images on every wall mark the temple as holy ground.

Tsela, side, and here side room. Eleven times in the chapter. It is the same word used for the rib or side taken from the man in Genesis 2:21-22, though here it refers simply to the chambers built along the sides of the temple.

christ: The New Testament reads the Most Holy Place in light of Christ. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). Hebrews explains that Christ entered not a sanctuary made with hands but heaven itself, as high priest, and that believers may now enter the holy places with confidence by his blood, through the curtain, his flesh (Hebrews 9:11-12, 24; 10:19-22). In Ezekiel's vision the prophet cannot go where the guide goes; in the gospel, Christ has gone in on behalf of his people and opened the way. The Eden imagery of the carvings also anticipates Revelation's new creation, where the tree of life stands beside the river and God's servants see his face (Revelation 22:1-4). These are thematic fulfillments, not a claim that Ezekiel foresaw the details.
questions: Ezekiel, though a priest, stays outside the Most Holy Place. What does that boundary teach about God, and how does the New Testament change it?
The walls are covered with cherubim and palm trees, reminders of Eden. Why might God want his house to recall the garden?
The last temple Ezekiel saw in vision was full of idols (chapter 8). What in your own life would need to be cleared out for it to become a place where God is honored?
